narrative:
The model estimated a 63.8% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that is above the threshold used for this decision, your law school application was rejected.

The strongest factor behind this prediction was your family-income background. Being in the middle-income bracket was associated with greater bar-exam risk in this data, especially compared with the upper-middle backgrounds that make up the largest share of accepted students. The second strongest factor was your first-year class standing. Your Year 1 decile was 5, below the accepted-student average of 6, so it also pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score was the third influence. At 39, it was slightly above the accepted-student average of about 37, but it was the weakest of the top three and still leaned the overall prediction toward failure rather than offsetting the other signals.

To improve your chances, ask the admissions office for specific feedback, strengthen your academic record where possible, consider retaking the LSAT only if practice tests show clear gains, and document legal experience, work responsibilities, or personal context that demonstrates readiness. Reapply when your file more convincingly shows you can pass the bar on the first try.
